title: Homily 17 on the Acts of the Apostles
breadcrumbs: Home > Fathers of the Church > Homilies on the Acts of the Apostles (Chrysostom) > Homily 17

paragraphs.text: Homily 17 on the Acts of the Apostles

<quote>This Moses whom they refused, saying, Who made you a ruler and a judge over us? The same did God send to be a ruler and a deliverer by the hand of the Angel which appeared to him in the bush.</quote>

This is very suitable to the matter in hand. <quote>This Moses,</quote> he says. <quote>This,</quote> the man who had been in danger of losing his life; the man who had been set at naught by them; <quote>this</quote> the man whom they had declined: <quote>this</quote> same, God having raised up, sent unto them. <quote>Whom they refused, saying, Who made you a ruler?</quote> just as they themselves (the hearers) said, <quote>We have no king, but Cæsar.</quote> {{BIBLE:joh 19:15}} He here shows also, that what was then done, was done by Christ. <quote>The same did God send by the hand of the Angel,</quote> who said unto him, <quote>I am the God of Abraham.</quote> <quote>This</quote> same Moses, he says—and observe how he points to his renown— <quote>this</quote> same Moses, he says, <quote>brought them out, after that he had showed wonders and signs in the land of Egypt, and in the Red sea, and in the wilderness forty years. This is that Moses, which said unto the children of Israel, A prophet shall the Lord your God raise up unto you of your brethren, like me</quote> (v. 36, 37): set at naught like me. Him, likewise, Herod wished to kill, and in Egypt He found preservation just as it was with the former, even when He was a babe, He was aimed at for destruction. <quote>This is he, that was in the Church in the wilderness with the Angel which spoke to him in the mount Sina, and with our fathers: who received the lively oracles to give unto us.</quote> {{BIBLE:act 7:38}} Again no mention of temple, none of sacrifice. <quote>With the Angel,</quote> it says, <quote>he received the lively oracles to give unto the fathers.</quote> It shows, that he not only wrought miracles, but also gave a law, as Christ did. Just as Christ first works miracles, and then legislates: so did Moses. But they did not hear him, keeping their disobedience, even after the miracles: <quote>To whom,</quote> he says, <quote>our fathers would not obey:</quote> {{BIBLE:act 7:39}} after the wonders done in those forty years. And not only so, but just the contrary: <quote>but thrust him from them, and in their hearts turned back again into Egypt. Saying unto Aaron, Make us gods to go before us; for as for this Moses, which brought us out of the land of Egypt, we know not what has become of him. And they made a calf in those days, and offered sacrifice unto the idol, and rejoiced in the works of their own hands. Then God turned, and gave them up to worship the host of heaven; as it is written in the book of the Prophets, O you house of Israel, have ye offered to me slain beasts and sacrifices by the space of forty years in the wilderness? Yea, you took up the tabernacle of Moloch, and the star of your god Remphan, figures which you made to worship them: and I will carry you away beyond Babylon.</quote> (v. 40, 43.) The expression, <quote>gave them up,</quote> means, He suffered. <quote>Our fathers had the tabernacle of witness in the wilderness, as he had appointed, speaking unto Moses, that he should make it according to the fashion he had seen.</quote> {{BIBLE:act 7:44}} Even when there was a Tabernacle, yet there were no sacrifices. <quote>Did ye offer unto Me slain beasts and sacrifices?</quote> {{BIBLE:amo 5:25}} There was <quote>the tabernacle of witness,</quote> and yet it profited them nothing, but they were consumed. But neither before, nor afterwards, did the miracles profit them anything. <quote>Which also, our fathers that came after brought in.</quote> Do you see, how the holy place is there wherever God may be? For to this end also he says, <quote>in the wilderness,</quote> to compare place with place. Then the benefit (conferred upon them): And our fathers that came after brought it in with Jesus into the possession of the Gentiles, whom God drove out before the face of our fathers, unto the days of David; who found favor before God, and desired to find a tabernacle for the God of Jacob. (v. 45, 46.) David <quote>desired to find favor:</quote> and he built not, he, the wonderful, the great; but the castaway, Solomon. <quote>But Solomon,</quote> it says, <quote>built Him an house. Howbeit the Most High dwells not in (places) made with hands.</quote> {{BIBLE:act 7:47}} This was shown indeed already by what had been before said: but it is shown also by the voice of a prophet; <quote>What house will you build for Me? Says the Lord God. As says the prophet, Heaven is my throne, and earth is my footstool: what house will you build for me? Says the Lord: or what is the place of my rest? Hath not my hand made all these things?</quote> {{BIBLE:isa 66:1}}

Marvel not, he says, if they on whom Christ confers His benefits refuse His kingdom, seeing in the case of Moses it was just the same. (Recapitulation). <quote>He brought them out;</quote> and rescued them not in a general way, but also while they were in the wilderness. <quote>Wonders and signs,</quote> etc. {{BIBLE:act 7:35}} Do you mark that they themselves (Stephen's hearers) are concerned in those old miracles also? <quote>This is that Moses:</quote> {{BIBLE:act 7:37}} he, that conversed with God; he, that had been saved out of situations so strange and wonderful; he, that wrought so great works, and had so great power. [<quote>Which said unto the children of Israel, A prophet,</quote> etc.] He shows, that the prophecy must by all means be fulfilled, and that Moses is not opposed to Him. <quote>This is he that was in the Church in the wilderness, and, that said unto the children of Israel.</quote> {{BIBLE:act 7:38}} Do you mark that thence comes the root, and that <quote>salvation is from the Jews?</quote> {{BIBLE:joh 4:22}} <quote>With the Angel,</quote> it says, <quote>which spoke unto him.</quote> {{BIBLE:rom 11:16}} Lo, again he affirms that it was He (Christ) that gave the Law, seeing Moses was with <quote>Him</quote> in the Church in the wilderness. And here he puts them in mind of a great marvel, of the things done in the Mount: <quote>Who received living oracles to give unto us.</quote> On all occasions Moses is wonderful, and (so) when need was to legislate. What means the expression, <quote>Living oracles</quote> (<greek>λόγια</greek>)? Those, whereof the end was shown by words (<greek>διὰ λόγων</greek>): in other words, he means the prophecies. Then follows the charge, in the first instance, against the patriarchs [after], the <quote>signs and wonders,</quote> after the receiving of the <quote>lively oracles: To whom,</quote> he says, <quote>our fathers would not obey.</quote> {{BIBLE:act 7:39}} But concerning those, Ezekiel says that they are not <quote>living;</quote> as when he says, <quote>And I gave you statutes that are not good.</quote> {{BIBLE:eze 20:25}} It is with reference to those that he says, <quote>Living. But thrust him from them, and in their hearts turned back to Egypt</quote>— the place where they groaned, where they cried, whence they called upon God. <quote>And said unto Aaron, Make us gods which shall go before us.</quote> {{BIBLE:act 7:40}} O the folly! <quote>Make,</quote> say they; <quote>that they may go before us.</quote> Whither? <quote>Into Egypt.</quote> See how hard they were to tear away from the customs of Egypt! What do you say? What, not wait for him that brought you out, but flee the benefit, and deny the Benefactor? And mark how insulting they are: <quote>For as for this Moses,</quote> they say:— <quote>which brought us out of the land of Egypt</quote> nowhere the name of God: instead of that, they ascribed all to Moses. Where they ought to give thanks (to God), they bring Moses forward: where it was, to do as the Law bade them, they no longer make account of Moses. <quote>We know not what has become of him.</quote> And yet he told them that he was going up to receive the Law: and they had not patience to wait forty days. <quote>Make us gods</quote>— they did not say, <quote>a God.</quote>— And yet one may well wonder at this, that they do not even know.— <quote>And they made a calf in those days, and offered sacrifices unto the idol, and rejoiced in the works of their own hands</quote> {{BIBLE:act 7:41}} : for which they ought to have hid their faces. What wonder that you know not Christ, seeing ye knew not Moses, and God Who was manifested by such wonders? But they not only knew Him not: they also insulted in another way, by their idol making. <quote>Then God turned, and gave them up to worship the host of heaven</quote> {{BIBLE:act 7:42}} Hence these same <quote>customs</quote> date their origin, hence the sacrifices: they were themselves the first that made sacrifices to their idols! For that is why it is marked, <quote>They made a calf in Horeb, and offered sacrifices to the idol:</quote> seeing that, before this the name of sacrifice is nowhere mentioned, but only lively ordinances, and <quote>lively oracles. And rejoiced</quote>— that is the reason for the feasts. {{BIBLE:exo 32:5}} <quote>As it is written in the Book of the Prophets</quote>— and observe, he does not cite the text without a purpose, but shows by it that there is no need of sacrifices; saying: <quote>Did ye offer slain beasts and sacrifice to Me?</quote>— He lays an emphasis on this word (to Me?). You cannot say that it was from sacrificing to Me, that you proceeded to sacrifice to them:— <quote>by the space of forty years:</quote> and this too, <quote>in the wilderness,</quote> where He had most signally shown Himself their Protector. <quote>Yea, you took up the tabernacle of Moloch, and the star of your god Remphan: images which you made to worship them.</quote> The cause of sacrifices! <quote>And I will carry you away beyond Babylon.</quote> {{BIBLE:act 7:43}} Even the captivity, an impeachment of their wickedness! <quote>But a Tabernacle,</quote> say you, <quote>there was (the Tabernacle) 'of Witness.'</quote> {{BIBLE:act 7:44}} (Yes,) this is why it was: that they should have God for Witness: this was all. <quote>According to the fashion,</quote> it says, <quote>that was shown you on the mount:</quote> so that on the mount was the Original. And this Tabernacle, moreover, <quote>in the wilderness,</quote> was carried about, and not locally fixed. And he calls it, <quote>Tabernacle of witness:</quote> i.e. (for witness) of the miracles, of the statutes. This is the reason why both it and those (the fathers) had no Temple. <quote>As He had appointed, that spoke unto Moses, that he should make it according to the fashion that he had seen.</quote> Again, it was none other than He (Christ) that gave the fashion itself. <quote>Until the days of David</quote> {{BIBLE:act 7:45}} : and there was no temple! And yet the Gentiles also had been driven out: for that is why he mentions this: <quote>Whom God drove out,</quote> he says, <quote>before the face of our fathers. Whom He drove out,</quote> he says: and even then, no Temple! And so many wonders, and no mention of a Temple! So that, although first there is a Tabernacle, yet nowhere a Temple. <quote>Until the days of David,</quote> he says: even David, and no Temple! <quote>And he sought to find favor before God</quote> {{BIBLE:act 7:46}} : and built not:— so far was the Temple from being a great matter! <quote>But Solomon built Him an house.</quote> {{BIBLE:act 7:47}} They thought Solomon was great: but that he was not better than his father, nay not even equal to him, is manifest. <quote>Howbeit the Most High dwells not in temples made with hands; as says the prophet, Heaven is My throne, and earth is My footstool.</quote> (v. 48, 49.) Nay, not even these are worthy of God, forasmuch as they are made, seeing they are creatures, the works of His hand. See how he leads them on little by little (showing) that not even these are to be mentioned. And again the prophecy says openly, <quote>What house will you build Me?</quote> etc. {{BIBLE:act 7:50}}

What is the reason that at this point he speaks in the tone of invective (<greek>καταφορικὥς</greek>)? Great was his boldness of speech, when at the point to die: for in fact I think he knew that this was the case. <quote>You stiffnecked,</quote> he says, <quote>and uncircumcised in heart and ears.</quote> This also is from the prophets: nothing is of himself. <quote>You do always resist the Holy Ghost: as your fathers did, so do ye.</quote> {{BIBLE:act 7:51}} When it was not His will that sacrifices should be, you sacrifice: when it is His will, then again ye do not sacrifice: when He would not give you commandments, you drew them to you: when you got them, you neglected them. Again, when the Temple stood, you worshipped idols: when it is His will to be worshipped without a Temple, you do the opposite. Observe, he says not, <quote>You resist God,</quote> but, <quote>the Spirit:</quote> so far was he from knowing any difference between Them. And, what is greater: <quote>As your fathers did,</quote> he says, <quote>so do ye.</quote> Thus also did Christ (reproach them), forasmuch as they were always boasting much of their fathers. <quote>Which of the prophets have not your fathers persecuted? And they have slain them which showed before of the coming of the Just One:</quote> he still says, <quote>the Just One,</quote> wishing to check them: <quote>of Whom you have been now the betrayers and murderers</quote>— two charges he lays against them — <quote>who have received the Law by the disposition of Angels, and have not kept it.</quote> {{BIBLE:act 7:52}} How, <quote>By the disposition of Angels?</quote> Some say (The Law), disposed by Angels; or, put into his hand by the Angel Who appeared to him in the bush; for was He man? No wonder that He who wrought those works, should also have wrought these. <quote>You slew them who preached of Him,</quote> much more Himself. He shows them disobedient both to God, and to Angels, and the Prophets, and the Spirit, and to all: as also Scripture says elsewhere: <quote>Lord, they have slain Your Prophets, and thrown down Your altars.</quote> {{BIBLE:1ki 19:10}} They, then, stand up for the Law, and say, <quote>He blasphemes against Moses:</quote> he shows, therefore, that it is they who blaspheme, and that (their blasphemy is not only against Moses, but) against God; shows that <quote>they</quote> from the very beginning have been doing this: that <quote>they</quote> have themselves destroyed their <quote>customs,</quote> that there is no need of these: that while accusing him, and saying that he opposed Moses, they themselves were opposing the Spirit: and not merely opposing, but with murder added to it: and that they had their enmity all along from the very beginning. Do you see, that he shows them to be acting in opposition both to Moses and to all others, and not keeping the Law? And yet Moses had said, A Prophet shall the Lord raise up unto you: and the rest also told of this (Christ) that He would come: and the prophet again said, <quote>What house will you build Me?</quote> and again, <quote>Did ye offer to Me slain beasts and sacrifices</quote> those <quote>forty years?</quote> {{BIBLE:deu 18:18}}

Such is the boldness of speech of a man bearing the Cross. Let us then also imitate this: though it be not a time of war, yet it is always the time for boldness of speech. For, <quote>I spoke,</quote> says one, <quote>in Your testimonies before kings, and was not ashamed.</quote> {{BIBLE:psa 118:46}} If we chance to be among heathens, let us thus stop their mouths. without wrath, without harshness. (Comp. Hom. in 1 Cor. iv. §6; xxxiii. §4, 5; Col. xi. §2.) For if we do it with wrath, it no longer seems to be the boldness (of one who is confident of his cause,) but passion: but if with gentleness, this is boldness indeed. For in one and the same thing success and failure cannot possibly go together. The boldness is a success: the anger is a failure. Therefore, if we are to have boldness, we must be clean from wrath that none may impute our words to that. No matter how just your words may be, when you speak with anger, you ruin all: no matter how boldly you speak, how fairly reprove, or what not. See this man, how free from passion as he discourses to them! For he did not abuse them: he did but remind them of the words of the Prophets. For, to show you that it was not anger, at the very moment he was suffering evil at their hands, he prayed, saying, <quote>Lay not to their charge this sin.</quote> So far was he from speaking these words in anger; no, he spoke in grief and sorrow for their sakes. As indeed this is why it speaks of his appearance, that <quote>they saw his face as it had been the face of an angel,</quote> on purpose that they might believe. Let us then be clean from wrath. The Holy Spirit dwells not where wrath is: cursed is the wrathful. It cannot be that anything wholesome should approach, where wrath goes forth. For as in a storm at sea, great is the tumult, loud the clamor, and then would be no time for lessons of wisdom (<greek>φιλοσοφεἵν</greek>): so neither in wrath. If the soul is to be in a condition either to say, or to be disciplined to, anything of philosophy, it must first be in the haven. Do you see not how, when we wish to converse on matters of serious import, we look out for places free from noise, where all is stillness, all calm, that we may not be put out and discomposed? But if noise from without discomposes, much more disturbance from within. Whether one pray, to no purpose does he pray <quote>with wrath and disputings:</quote> {{BIBLE:1ti 2:8}} whether he speak, he will only make himself ridiculous: whether he hold his peace, so again it will be even then: whether he eat, he is hurt even then: whether he drink, or whether he drink not; whether he sit, or stand, or walk; whether he sleep: for even in their dreams such fancies haunt them. For what is there in such men that is not disagreeable? Eyes unsightly, mouth distorted, limbs agitated and swollen, tongue foul and sparing no man, mind distraught, gestures uncomely: much to disgust. Mark the eyes of demoniacs, and those of drunkards and madmen; in what do they differ from each other? Is not the whole madness? For what though it be but for the moment? The madman too is possessed for the moment: but what is worse than this? And they are not ashamed at that excuse; <quote>I knew not (says one) what I said.</quote> And how came it that thou did not know this, thou the rational man, you that hast the gift of reason, on purpose that you may not act the part of the creatures without reason, just like a wild horse, hurried away by rage and passion? In truth, the very excuse is criminal. For you ought to have known what you said. <quote>It was the passion,</quote> say you, <quote>that spoke the words, not I.</quote> How should it be that? For passion has no power, except it get it from you. You might as well say, <quote>It was my hand that inflicted the wounds, not I.</quote> What occasion, think you, most needs wrath? Would you not say, war and battle? But even then, if anything is done with wrath, the whole is spoiled and undone. For of all men, those who fight had best not be enraged: of all men, those had best not be enraged, who want to hurt (<greek>τοὺς ὑβρίζοντας</greek>). And how is it possible to fight then? You will ask. With reason, with self-command (<greek>ἐ</greek> <greek>πιεικεί& 139
